transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-03 11:00 PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (CTO - Matador), Priya Shah (Lead ML Eng), Tom Ng (SRE)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect):
Matador Labs is evaluating Redwood for a mix of hosted and private (VPC) usage. Primary driver is a hard monthly cost ceiling for per-token spend. Key constraints: 1) average request context ~800–1,200 tokens, 2) peak concurrency 120 req/s for short bursts, 3) strict data residency + KMS for keys. Discussed batching, KV/prefix caching, reserved capacity discounts, and tradeoffs for dedicated vs hosted for predictable unit economics. Next steps: pricing sheet, security docs, engineer-to-engineer benchmark with sample prompts.

Topics: costs vs latency, batching and caching levers, hosted discounts and dedicated guarantees, private VPC considerations, pilot scope and sample benchmarks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Maya from Redwood. I think we have about 45 minutes on the calendar, is that still good?
[00:06] Carlos Rivera: Yep that's perfect. Got my team here, Priya and Tom. We're the, uh, evaluating cost mainly, so we appreciate the time.
[00:12] Priya Shah: Hi, Maya. Hi Jordan. Quick note — we did send a rough token log earlier in the week, hopefully that landed.
[00:17] Maya Patel: Yes, we received it, thank you. Jordan, do you want to kick us off on the economics side and then we can go into deployment options?
[00:23] Jordan Lee: Sure. So high-level — Redwood offers a hosted API with per-token pricing, and then Dedicated which is reserved GPU pools with committed throughput, and Private which is a VPC/on-prem control plane option. From a unit econ perspective the levers you have are: batching (increases throughput and lowers per-token inference cost), KV/prefix caching to avoid re-computing shared context, and model quantization/variant selection.
[00:41] Tom Ng: When you say batching, are you referring to automatic batching at the runtime or something we need to build into our client?
[00:46] Jordan Lee: Automatic continuous batching is in the runtime — Redwood will batch compatible requests to maximize GPU utilization. There are also knobs you can set on a per-route basis to favor latency vs batch size.
[00:56] Carlos Rivera: Ok, our main concern is we've got a monthly token budget ceiling. We can't exceed X dollars per month — that cap is non-negotiable. So two things: how reliably can you bound our spend and how much can we reduce per-token through batching/caching?
[01:10] Jordan Lee: Got it. Bounding spend — if you go Dedicated with a reserved slot count and committed throughput we can guarantee capacity and predictable monthly billing. Hosted has metered per-token bills but we offer rate-limiting and alerts; you can also set hard quotas. For many customers we do a hybrid: hosted for dev and low-volume, dedicated for production-critical workloads to hit a predictable unit cost.
[01:29] Priya Shah: Curious — what's the typical delta in unit cost between hosted and dedicated? Ballpark numbers are fine.
[01:34] Maya Patel: Ballpark — depends a lot on model size and sequence lengths. For a 30B-ish open model, hosted per-token might be around $0.00023 per prompt token and $0.00023 per completion token for some tiers (rough example), while Dedicated pricing after reservation and utilization can be 20–40% lower per-token. If you can leverage caching and batching effectively you can push that further.
[01:57] Carlos Rivera: That matches roughly what we saw with other vendors. The issue for us is our context lengths — average 900 tokens, sometimes up to 2k. That eats tokens fast.
[02:06] Jordan Lee: Right. Two levers there: prefix/KV caching — if most of the 900 tokens are shared system/context tokens, we can avoid re-sending them to the model every request and re-use cached KV state; that can drop your effective per-request tokens by 40–70% depending on how much is shared. Second is choosing a model variant with efficient attention kernels and enabling quantization where accuracy is acceptable.
[02:27] Priya Shah: How often do customers see that 40–70%? That seems optimistic.
[02:31] Jordan Lee: It is optimistic as an upper bound. More realistic if you're doing RAG with a stable prompt prefix is 20–45% on average. The key is workload characteristics — if you can isolate the stable prefix (system instruction, user persona, etc.) we get big wins.
[02:44] Tom Ng: On caching — for our compliance needs we can't store PII in the cache. Is that doable?
[02:49] Jordan Lee: Yes — you can configure what goes into KV cache. We also have data classification hooks. For Private/VPC deployments you can choose to have the cache only in your VPC so we never see it; for Hosted we support encryption at rest and redaction pipelines.
[03:03] Carlos Rivera: That brings me to keys — we need KMS integration. Can your private offering use our KMS/HSM?
[03:09] Maya Patel: Yes, for Private deployments you can bring your own KMS. For Dedicated we offer KMS integrations too; for Hosted we provide customer-managed keys via supported cloud KMS options. We'll include the KMS docs in the security pack.
[03:22] Priya Shah: Great. Back to budgeting — do you support a token forecasting model so we can set early alerts before we hit the monthly cap?
[03:29] Jordan Lee: We do. Console can project burn rate using current throughput and historical patterns. We also send alert webhooks and can enforce hard quotas at the API layer. Many customers run a 'guardrail' project that throttles noncritical traffic when near cap.
[03:42] Carlos Rivera: Any gotchas with batching — like increases in latency tails when batching for throughput?
[03:47] Jordan Lee: Yes, batching trades off latency for cost. Our runtime supports latency SLOs — you can set a latency target and the runtime will favor small batches to meet it. Conversely, if you can accept slightly higher p95, we'll batch more aggressively and reduce token cost. There's also per-route config: low-latency routes can be pinned to dedicated GPU lanes.
[04:04] Priya Shah: Do you have any built-in tooling that suggests batch sizes or quantization settings based on our logs?
[04:11] Maya Patel: Redwood Optimize will analyze traffic patterns and recommend batching and quantization profiles to hit target cost/latency tradeoffs. It can suggest reserved capacity sizing too. We'll demo that in the pilot.
[04:22] Tom Ng: About pilot — what would you expect from us to run a meaningful benchmark?
[04:26] Jordan Lee: Ideally: 1) a representative prompt set, 2) sample throughput patterns (burst vs steady), 3) a few golden outputs for quality checks, and 4) any redaction rules so we can emulate your privacy constraints. Priya mentioned token logs — that's perfect.
[04:41] Priya Shah: We'll pull a week of anonymized logs and the prompt set. One question — embeddings are a huge driver for us, too. How are embeddings priced and can they be cached?
[04:52] Maya Patel: Embeddings are priced per vector compute unit (we bill per-embedding call). You can cache embeddings for documents in an external vector DB; Redwood doesn't automatically persist user embeddings for hosted use unless you enable persistence. For Private deployments, you can choose to keep the embeddings local in your VPC. Caching embeddings reduces calls but doesn't reduce model decode cost since embeddings are separate.
[05:12] Carlos Rivera: Are there any minimum commitments for Dedicated?
[05:15] Maya Patel: There's a minimum monthly commit depending on GPU class; we'll outline exact numbers in the pricing sheet. Commitments typically align with your expected throughput — customers often do a 3–12 month reserved plan.
[05:26] Priya Shah: For our ROI case, we need a confidence interval on cost per 1k end-user interactions. Do you have a quick calc we can do in the call?
[05:34] Jordan Lee: We can do a worked example. If your average request total is 1,000 tokens and you make 100k interactions a month, that's 100M tokens. On hosted at say $0.00023/token, that's $23k. If Dedicated reduces unit cost by 30% that's $16.1k. Now if caching removes 30% of tokens effective that's another drop to ~11k. These are rough numbers but show the lever multiplicative effects — pick the sequence length, multiply by interactions, apply effective cache reduction, then the per-token price after reserved discount.
[06:10] Tom Ng: That sensitivity is helpful. But we also have burst concurrency needs — 120 req/s for 2–3 minute windows. Do you support burst autoscaling?
[06:19] Maya Patel: Yes. Dedicated can be configured with burst pools that spin up extra capacity; Hosted also supports burst capacity but it's subject to regional availability. There's a cost to the burst buffer but it's cheaper than overprovisioning permanently.
[06:31] Carlos Rivera: What about failover — if Dedicated pool is saturated, do you have fallback to hosted and what's the cost implication?
[06:38] Jordan Lee: We support automated fallback policies — you can fall back to a hosted-compatible model variant. We surface the differences in latency and unit cost in the Console so you can make a tradeoff decision; we also do canary rollouts to avoid big surprises.
[06:52] Priya Shah: Security + compliance — we need SOC 2, ISO, and audit logs for every request that hits the model. Is that available for both Hosted and Dedicated?
[06:59] Maya Patel: SOC 2 and ISO certifications apply to our control plane and hosted offering; for Dedicated and Private, you get detailed audit logging and you can forward logs to your SIEM. For Private on-prem, you're in control of the logs. We'll send the security pack with specifics on log retention and export.
[07:13] Tom Ng: A practical question — how long does a Private deployment take to stand up?
[07:18] Jordan Lee: Depends on environment — VPC Private deployment is typically 4–8 weeks including network review and KMS provisioning; air-gapped on-prem can take longer. We have a playbook and an SOW for that.
[07:28] Carlos Rivera: We like the hybrid idea. Dev and non-sensitive functions on Hosted, production PII flows in Private. How do we route between them?
[07:35] Jordan Lee: Smart routing policies in the control plane can route requests by policy (region, model, sensitivity tags). You can label routes as 'sensitive' and they will be forced into your Private endpoints. The control plane will also handle fallback to compatible variants.
[07:48] Priya Shah: Any material differences in model versions between Hosted and Private? Like will we always get the same model weights?
[07:54] Jordan Lee: We maintain a model catalog; generally same model variants are available but there may be slight timing differences for newest releases. For Private we also support pinned versions so you can lock to a specific weight.
[08:05] Carlos Rivera: Okay — paperwork. We'll need a pricing estimate and the SLA terms to go to procurement.
[08:10] Maya Patel: We'll send the pricing tiers and a sample SLA. Also we'll include options for pilot discounts and a 3-month committed pilot if you want predictable spend while evaluating.
[08:20] Tom Ng: For the benchmark session, who will lead it? Engineer-to-engineer preferred.
[08:25] Jordan Lee: I'll lead the bench run and work with Priya to integrate your prompt set. We'll run both hosted and a dedicated sim to compare cost and latency under your workload.
[08:34] Priya Shah: Perfect. One more nit — how do you charge for context window when you use KV cache?
[08:40] Jordan Lee: If KV cache is used effectively, the billing still counts tokens decoded by the model; cached KV avoids recomputation, so those tokens are not billed per-request. However, initial cache priming ops and cache population will be billed. We'll document that nuance in the pricing note.
[08:55] Carlos Rivera: Any vendor lock-in concerns when using caching and dedicated optimizations?
[09:00] Maya Patel: We try to minimize lock-in — caches are transparent and configurable, and you can export cache state. Dedicated uses standard model formats; if you ever move, we provide export tools. But yes, any heavy optimization can increase migration complexity — we'll outline that in the pilot SOW.
[09:12] Priya Shah: Ok good. Let's do a quick recap and next steps.
[09:16] Maya Patel: Recap: Redwood will send pricing sheet, security pack (SOC2, KMS, audit logs), and a bench runbook. Matador will provide anonymized token logs and a representative prompt set. Jordan will schedule a 90-minute engineer bench with Priya and Tom in ~2 weeks. Action items and due dates to follow in email.
[09:36] Carlos Rivera: Sounds good. Any final questions?
[09:39] Tom Ng: None from me. Thanks.
[09:41] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up and send the materials.
